Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims of reviewing submissions, brazen rating manipulation on the App Store remains undetected.

He says that, although he doesn't actively search for scam apps on the App Store, he often encounters them by chance, and shared a recent example...

App Store is a "safe and trusted place"

Apple has taken a hard line against any antitrust measures involving third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, often only relenting when forced by law. Even so, Apple continues to defend itself.

The company claims it does so not for money, but to protect iPhone users from malware. For example, Apple said last year that it had blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers question the claim that the "App Store is a safe place," pointing to numerous scam cases involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who claimed their Bitcoin was completely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store rating manipulation

App Store rating manipulation has been a long-standing problem, with companies even renting "iPhone farms" in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for the StopTheMadness Safari extension) noted that he believes the latest case of App Store review manipulation is "large-scale and obvious." The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He says that when he stumbled upon this app, it was ranked 12th on the US Mac App Store paid Safari extensions chart, and the screenshots displayed were clearly AI-generated fake images.

Another notable point is that the fake screenshot claims the app has a "4.9 rating (out of 5)," misleading people into thinking these are ratings from App Store users...Using App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself, but also the App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam apps' screenshots are often absurd to the extreme, yet Apple routinely approves them...Apple claims the App Store can protect users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even detect these kinds of problems, then what's the point? In fact, App Store review doesn't need to dig as deep as I did. A screenshot claiming a "4.9 rating (out of 5)" is itself a red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews for every country, so they know full well this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the damn app to know the developer is trying to deceive users.

As he says, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics from the very start to sell their app, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, completely eradicating all App Store scams is impossible, but fake reviews are extremely common, and cases like this one should be blatantly obvious to Apple. What's puzzling is how this extension managed to pass review in the first place.

Apple should at the very least establish a mechanism to automatically subject any app that makes it onto the charts to more rigorous review, checking both the app itself and the claims it makes.
